Neonates of the Marsh rice rat (Oryzomys palustris) typically weigh between 3 and 4 grams (3-4 grams) [Wwb = 3-4 grams] at birth, a modest mass that reflects the altricial state of the newborn pups. Under the stable thermal conditions of the maternal nest, approximately 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], the gestation period lasts for about 25 days [tg = about 25 days], a duration that is relatively brief compared to many other cricetid rodents of comparable body size. This short intrauterine development is consistent with the species' rapid life-history strategy, which is adapted to fluctuating wetland environments where high mortality rates among young select for accelerated reproductive schedules. The altricial neonates are born blind and sparsely furred, entirely dependent on maternal care for thermoregulation and nutrition. Field studies indicate that the wet weight at birth can vary with maternal condition and litter size, but the reported range of 3 to 4 grams (3-4 grams) [Wwb = 3-4 grams] is consistently observed in populations across the southeastern United States. This initial mass represents a critical investment by the dam, as it must support the pup through the first days of life before nursing establishes a reliable energy supply.

The Marsh rice rat exhibits a maximum reproductive rate that is notably high for a small mammal inhabiting temperate salt marshes. At a body temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], the potential for multiple litters per year is substantial. The typical litter size ranges from 1 to 7 pups per litter [N_R_i = 1 to 7 pups per litter], and females can produce approximately 6 litters each year [F_R_i = approximately 6 litters each year] — a combination that yields a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 0.082 pups per day [Ri = approximately 0.082 pups per day], calculated as the product of litter size and yearly frequency divided by 365. This high reproductive potential is ecologically significant, as it compensates for the short lifespan and high predation pressure characteristic of coastal marsh ecosystems. Litter size is influenced by maternal age and nutritional status, with older, heavier females tending to produce larger litters within the 1-7 pup range. The seasonal timing of breeding is closely tied to photoperiod and resource availability, with peak reproductive activity occurring during the warmer months.

Weaning in the Marsh rice rat occurs relatively early in postnatal development, reflecting the species' rapid ontogenetic trajectory. Under the thermoneutral conditions of the nest at 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], the time since birth at weaning is approximately 15 days after birth [tx = approximately 15 days after birth], with a range of 11 to 20 days reported from captive colonies. This early nutritional independence is facilitated by the mother's rich milk and the rapid development of the digestive system in the pups. By this stage, the young have opened their eyes, developed a full coat of fur, and are capable of locomoting independently, although they continue to remain near the natal burrow for shelter. The pre-weaning juvenile period is a critical window during which altricial dependent young transition from a diet of milk to solid foods, such as seeds and invertebrates. The weaning process involves a gradual reduction in nursing frequency rather than an abrupt cessation, allowing the pups to acclimate to exogenous feeding sources. This dietary transition is essential for the attainment of nutritional independence prior to dispersal.

Female Marsh rice rats reach sexual maturity rapidly, in keeping with the species' r-selected life history. The time since birth at puberty for females is 55 days since birth [tp = 55 days since birth], with a documented range of 50 to 60 days reported in laboratory populations maintained at a regulated temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. This early onset of reproductive maturity means that females born early in the breeding season can themselves reproduce within the same year, contributing to the potential for population irruptions under favorable conditions. The attainment of puberty is marked by the first ovulation and the opening of the vaginal orifice, signs that are easily monitored in captive settings. In wild populations, the exact timing of first reproduction may be delayed by nutritional constraints or social factors, but the physiological capacity for early maturation remains a key adaptation. This precocious reproductive development contrasts with that of many larger-bodied murid rodents, which require several months to reach sexual maturity. The rapid maturation of the Marsh rice rat is a central component of its life-history strategy, enabling it to exploit ephemeral resources.

The ultimate wet weight of the Marsh rice rat, representing the maximum adult body mass, averages around 60 grams [Wwi = around 60 grams] across much of its range, although individuals can vary from 40 to 80 grams depending on geographic location and habitat quality. This adult body mass is modest even by cricetid standards, placing the species among the smaller members of its genus. In contrast to its rapid development, the maximum lifespan recorded for this species is relatively short: free-living individuals rarely survive beyond one year, and the typical life span under natural conditions is approximately 365 days [am = approximately 365 days] when maintained at a core body temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. The juxtaposition of a modest adult mass with a short life span and high fecundity underscores the species' position as a fast-living strategist adapted to unpredictable marsh habitats. Comparative studies with congeneric species such as Oryzomys couesi reveal similar patterns of rapid growth and early senescence. The ultimate wet weight is achieved within a few months of birth, after which growth slows considerably. This life-history syndrome is typical of small mammals that experience high extrinsic mortality.
